comments.body:
## AC1 answer from the reading done during the 9ea3 investigation — an index already exists; building one is NOT the fix

AC1 asks why the fall-through to `_scan_alias` happens before an index is designed. Worth answering before any design, because the obvious fix does not work.

**An alias index already exists and is already public.** `build_alias_index(tracker_dir)` is defined at `src/rebar/_ids.py:276` and re-exported from `src/rebar/_engine_support/resolver.py:31` (and named in its `__all__` at `:49`). This is not a missing capability.

**Why it is not used.** `alias_index` is a per-call, caller-supplied keyword argument on `resolve_ticket_id` (`_ids.py:411`), consulted at `_ids.py:457-460`:

    alias_matches = (
        alias_index.get(ticket_id, [])
        if alias_index is not None
        else _scan_alias(ticket_id, tracker_dir)
    )

There is **no store-level cache behind it** — nothing persists or memoizes the index between calls. The only caller that builds one is `_engine_support/commit_impact.py:213-214`, which does so precisely because it resolves MANY ids in one operation (it even times the build: `alias_index_build_ms`). Every other caller — every MCP tool and CLI command resolving a single id — passes nothing and takes `_scan_alias`.

**The trap for the next investigator: building the index on demand would fix nothing.** `build_alias_index` costs the same full-store walk `_scan_alias` does — both must read every ticket's CREATE/SNAPSHOT to compute its effective alias. Building an index to serve ONE resolution is exactly as expensive as scanning for that one alias. The index only pays when amortized across many resolutions inside a single call, which is why `commit_impact` is its only user and why the single-id path was left alone.

So the shape of the real fix is **not** "add an index" but one of:

1. **Persist/cache the index across calls**, keyed by the ticket-store revision (the store is event-sourced, so its HEAD is a natural key), paying the walk once per store change instead of once per resolution; or
2. **Maintain an alias -> dir map on WRITE**, so no read path ever derives it.

**The correctness constraint on either.** `_effective_alias_for_dir` exists because an alias can be re-pointed — a directory's *effective* alias is not simply whatever its CREATE said. Any cache or maintained map must reproduce that shadowing exactly, which is why this ticket's AC3 differential check over the real store is the load-bearing part, not the index.

**One more datum for the ordering question.** In `resolve_ticket_id`, alias is the LAST form tried before prefix resolution: full canonical id, two-quad short id and Jira key are all handled earlier and cheaply (`_ids.py:442-455`). The cost is specific to the alias form — which is the form `AGENTS.md` instructs agents to prefer writing. The documented-preferred id form is the only one without an index. That is the defect in one sentence, and it is why it hits agent traffic rather than scripted use.

(Recorded from the 9ea3 investigation per the request to comment rather than let this be re-derived. Not taking this ticket. Posted via the local CLI: the MCP server was returning 300s idle timeouts and then disconnected — the same failure this ticket documents.)

comments.body:
## Measurement that partly CHALLENGES this ticket's cost attribution — read the caveat first

Orchestrator ran a three-form comparison on the SAME ticket, this store, via the local CLI:

```
alias  lousy-unsuited-gnu       43.01 s
short  94c5-b42e                36.51 s
full   94c5-b42e-ac80-4f06      36.26 s
```

### What this DOES establish

Alias resolution costs measurably more than the indexed forms — about **6.7 s, ~18%** — which
independently corroborates that alias is the last form tried and the only one without an index.
Short and full id are within 0.25 s of each other, consistent with both being handled by the cheap
earlier paths.

### What it does NOT establish, and why the caveat matters

A **full canonical id still costs 36.3 s**. If `_scan_alias` were the dominant term — the ticket's
framing is "~8,900 parses to resolve one id, making a single-ticket read ~2.5x a whole-store
compile" — then a full-id read, which never reaches `_scan_alias`, should have been dramatically
cheaper. It is not. Roughly 36 s is present regardless of id form.

**This test is CONFOUNDED and cannot settle where that 36 s goes.** All three numbers include CLI
cold start: process spawn, Python imports, and the store load, none of which the warm MCP server
pays. So the 36 s floor may be CLI overhead rather than resolution, and the ticket's 41.7 s figure
was measured through MCP, not the CLI. The two are not directly comparable. Only the DELTA between
forms (6.7 s) is a controlled comparison here, because cold start is common to all three.

### What should be measured before designing the fix

AC3 asks for single-ticket read latency well under the ~60 s client deadline. Whether that is
achievable by fixing resolution ALONE depends on the split this test could not make:

1. In-process (no CLI spawn), time `resolve_ticket_id` alone for each id form, and separately time
   the read that follows it. That isolates resolution from everything else.
2. If resolution is only a modest fraction of a warm single-ticket read, then persisting an alias
   index — the direction AC1 correctly identifies, since `build_alias_index` already exists at
   `_ids.py:276` and costs the same full-store walk, so building it on demand fixes nothing — will
   NOT by itself bring the read under the deadline, and the ticket needs a second cause.
3. If resolution IS dominant when measured warm, the index direction stands as written.

Recording this so the fix is not scoped against an unverified attribution. The ticket's mechanism
(alias unindexed, last tried, documented-preferred form) is confirmed; its share of total latency
is not.

### Practical note

An interim "have agents pass ids instead of aliases" mitigation was considered and is NOT worth
pursuing on this evidence: ~18% on the CLI, against AGENTS.md's explicit guidance to prefer aliases
in tracker commands. Not a good trade for a workaround. The in-flight cleanup driver was left
running untouched for the same reason — it already records canonical ids alongside aliases, and
disrupting a checkpointed 389-ticket run for a possible ~15% is not justified.

comments.body:
## AC1 / AC2 / AC5 — measured mechanism and before/after

### PROVEN: the ~8,900-parse claim is correct, and it is specific to the ALIAS form

In-process instrumentation (`json.load` counted, real store, 8,920-8,936 ticket dirs):

| id form | token | `json.load` calls | file opens |
|---|---|---|---|
| full canonical | `94c5-b42e-ac80-4f06` | **0** | 0 |
| 8-digit two-quad short | `94c5-b42e` | **0** | 0 |
| alias | `lousy-unsuited-gnu` | **8,920** | 8,921 |
| deprecated 4-digit quad | `94c5` | **8,920** | 8,920 |

The 4-digit fragment pays it too: `resolve_ticket_id` tries the alias branch
BEFORE prefix resolution, so the fragment eats a full alias scan on its way to a
`bisect`-able prefix match.

`show_ticket` resolves TWICE per call (`_engine_support/reads.py:344` →
`resolve_ticket_id`, plus `_lib_warn.emit_cross_session_warning` →
`_commands/cross_session.py:33`), so one alias-form read did **17,844** parses.
cProfile of `show_ticket("lousy-unsuited-gnu")`: `_scan_alias` = 3.218 s of a
3.400 s call — **95%**.

### Mechanism, cited

`_scan_alias` (`src/rebar/_ids.py:312`) lists the tracker root and calls
`_effective_alias_for_dir` (`src/rebar/_ids.py:171`) per ticket dir; that helper
does one `os.listdir` + one `open` + one `json.load` of the CREATE (or SNAPSHOT)
event. `resolve_ticket_id` reaches it at the alias branch
(`src/rebar/_ids.py:457-461`) whenever no caller supplied `alias_index=`.

The earlier CLI three-form comparison on this ticket (43.0 s alias vs 36.3 s
full, "only ~18%") was, as that comment itself warned, confounded by CLI cold
start. Measured warm and in-process the split is **25x**, not 18%. That comment's
caveat was right to demand the in-process split; the split confirms the ticket's
original attribution rather than challenging it.

### REFUTED: the name-derived shortcut

`_effective_alias_for_dir` falls back to `compute_alias(dir_name)`, so a
zero-I/O shortcut looked plausible. It is not: **7,993 of 8,920** ticket dirs
have a stored alias that differs from the name-derived one (alias wordlist drift
across store history). Stored aliases must be read from disk.

### Fix and before/after

Process-local memo of the existing `ResolverScanIndex`, revalidated by one
`os.scandir` pass over `(name, st_mtime_ns)` — no `open`, no `json.load`. Same
index the `alias_index=` parameter already accepts, so match sets and ambiguity
behaviour are unchanged.

Measured on the real store, same host, same window:

| operation | before | after (steady state) |
|---|---|---|
| `resolve_ticket_id` alias — `json.load` calls | 8,920 | **0** |
| `resolve_ticket_id` alias — latency | 6,576 ms | **84 ms** |
| `resolve_ticket_id` 4-digit quad — latency | 4,422 ms | **53-77 ms** |
| `resolve_ticket_id` short / full id | 41 ms / 0 ms | 8-14 ms / 0 ms (unchanged path) |
| `show_ticket(alias)` | 7.6 / 17.8 / 8.2 s | **0.166 s** |
| `show_ticket(full id)` | 0.48 s | 0.072 s |

(An earlier, quieter-host baseline measured `show_ticket(alias)` at 2.959 s and
alias resolve at 1,313 ms; the host was contended for the paired run above. The
parse COUNT — 17,844 → 0 — is the load-independent invariant.)

First resolution in a fresh process still pays one full store pass (7.2 s cold
page cache); every subsequent one is free until the store changes. That is the
whole win for the MCP server, which is long-lived. Persisting the index ACROSS
processes — which would also help one-shot CLI invocations — is deliberately out
of scope here.

### AC4 semantics tests (`tests/unit/test_single_id_alias_resolve_scan_cache.py`)

Full canonical id, 8-digit two-quad short id, alias, Jira/bridge key via the
binding store, deprecated 4-digit fragment, unknown tokens, ambiguous-alias
refusal (with its stderr diagnostic), invalidation on ticket creation, and
invalidation on an alias change made INSIDE an existing ticket dir (the
compaction shape: CREATE retired, SNAPSHOT `compiled_state.alias` takes over) —
the last one covering the plan review's advisory `fc80ba265576e3f6d`.

Portability note for the review's mtime-granularity advisory
(`fff2d80a9310de4a5`): the fingerprint has two independent components. The
ticket-directory NAME SET is timestamp-free, and creating a ticket — the only
operation that introduces a new alias — necessarily adds a directory, so new
aliases are detected on any filesystem regardless of mtime granularity. The
per-directory mtime is the secondary signal covering in-place alias-source
changes.

## Change 2723 is double-green; local `make verify` is blocked by an unrelated host defect

Gerrit change: https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/2723
`LLM-Review +1` (rebar review bot) and `Verified +1` (rebar CI bot), 0 unresolved
comments, `submittable: true`. Not submitted — left for the operator.

### Local `make verify` — what actually happened

Three runs on this host, same commit: lint and typecheck green every time
(including the complexity and mechanism-delta ratchets), and 19,873-19,884 tests
passing. Every failure in every run was
`GateCongestedError: gate admission refused: all 4 concurrent slots busy`, with a
DIFFERENT failure set each run (15 / 9 / 26).

Root cause is NOT this change. `make test` runs pytest `-n 4`, and the gate
admission cap is 4 slots that are HOST-GLOBAL — `_slot_dir()`
(`src/rebar/llm/gate_admission.py:210`) puts them under the snapshot store root's
`locks/`, shared by every rebar process on the box. During one run the holder was
captured directly:

    60942 /Users/joeoakhart/scanner-promote/.venv/bin/rebar review-plan
          guileless-emeritus-izuthrush

— another worktree's plan review. Each affected test passes when run alone, and
the same multi-file selection passes on unmodified `main`. Filed as
`careful-liberal-skua` (e5eb-ef5e-c10a-4729), linked `discovered_from` this
ticket.

CI's `Verified +1` on this exact commit — an isolated runner with no competing
rebar processes — is the authoritative signal that the suite is green.

### Scope note

The fix caches the resolver index PER PROCESS. A long-lived process (the MCP
server) pays one store pass and then resolves for free; a one-shot CLI invocation
still pays that pass once, though `show_ticket` benefits immediately because it
resolves twice per call. Persisting the index ACROSS processes would also help
one-shot CLI use and is deliberately not attempted here.

compiled_state.description:
## Summary

Resolving a ticket by ALIAS falls through to `_scan_alias` (`src/rebar/_ids.py:312`), which
`os.listdir`s the tracker root and, for EVERY ticket dir, calls `_effective_alias_for_dir`
(`src/rebar/_ids.py:171`) — one `listdir` + one `open` + one `json.load` per ticket. On this
store that is ~8,900 JSON parses to resolve ONE id, and `show_ticket` resolves twice per call.

## Confirmed measurements (in-process, warm page cache, this store: 8,920 ticket dirs)

| operation | latency | `json.load` calls |
|---|---|---|
| `resolve_ticket_id("94c5-b42e-ac80-4f06")` (full) | 0.0 ms | 0 |
| `resolve_ticket_id("94c5-b42e")` (short) | 5.7 ms | 0 |
| `resolve_ticket_id("lousy-unsuited-gnu")` (alias) | 1313 ms | 8,920 |
| `resolve_ticket_id("94c5")` (deprecated 4-digit) | 1375 ms | 8,920 |
| `show_ticket(full id)` | 119 ms | — |
| `show_ticket(alias)` | 2,959 ms | 17,844 |

cProfile of `show_ticket(alias)`: `_scan_alias` is 3.218 s of 3.400 s cumulative — **95% of the
call**. The earlier CLI-based comparison on this ticket (43.0 s alias vs 36.3 s full) was
confounded by CLI cold start, as that comment itself flagged; measured in-process the split is
25x, not 18%.

## AC1 answer — why the fall-through happens

`build_resolver_scan_index` / `build_alias_index` already exist (`_ids.py:262`, `:276`) but are
per-call, caller-supplied arguments. The only caller that builds one is
`_engine_support/commit_impact.py`, which resolves many ids per operation. There is **no cache
behind them**, so every single-id resolution scans. Building the index on demand for one
resolution costs exactly what the scan costs, so "add an index" is not the fix.

A shortcut via `compute_alias(dir_name)` is also ruled out by measurement: 7,993 of 8,920 ticket
dirs have a stored alias that differs from the name-derived one (wordlist drift), so stored
aliases must be read from disk.

## Fix

Memoize the resolver scan index **per process, per tracker dir**, validated by a cheap
fingerprint of the tracker root: for each ticket dir, `(name, st_mtime_ns)` from one `os.scandir`
pass — no `open`, no `json.load`. Measured: fingerprint 87-110 ms vs index build 2,953 ms (~30x).
Any event file appended to a ticket dir bumps that dir's mtime, and any ticket added or removed
changes the root entry set, so the fingerprint changes whenever any input to an effective alias
could have changed. On a fingerprint miss the index is rebuilt exactly as today.

The cached index is the SAME `ResolverScanIndex` the existing `alias_index=` path already
consumes, so match sets and ambiguity handling are byte-identical to the per-call scan. The cache
is process-local state only (no config key, no env var, no lock, no on-disk artifact).

Scope: `src/rebar/_ids.py` only. Persisting the index across processes (which would also help
one-shot CLI invocations) is deliberately out of scope and will be filed separately if wanted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 The fall-through to `_scan_alias` is explained: which id FORMS reach it, and whether a
      faster path already exists that is not being consulted. Recorded as a comment.
- [x] AC2 A RED test demonstrates the pathological cost — K single-id alias resolutions against
      an unchanged store must not cost K full-store passes — and fails before the fix.
- [x] AC3 Repeated single-ticket reads in one process no longer re-parse the whole store;
      demonstrated by a measured before/after on a store of this size, not a fixture.
- [x] AC4 Resolution remains CORRECT across every accepted id form — full canonical id, 8-digit
      two-quad short id, alias, Jira/bridge key, and the deprecated 4-digit fragment — plus
      ambiguity detection and cache invalidation on ticket creation, each pinned by test.
- [x] AC5 The measured before/after latency table is recorded on this ticket.

## Constraints

Never use `--force` or any gate bypass. `timeout` does not exist on this macOS host (exit 127) —
bound with `perl -e 'alarm N; exec @ARGV'`. Do not touch the shared main checkout; do not
`git stash` anywhere. Respect the 800-LOC module cap (`_ids.py` is 496), the shrink-only
complexity ratchet, and the mechanism-delta ratchet.
